text: Figure phb_prevalence_by_phylum.png plots PHB pathway prevalence across 20 major bacterial phyla.
quote: ![PHB pathway prevalence across 20 major bacterial phyla, showing Pseudomonadota, Myxococcota, and Halobacteriota as the most enriched](figures/phb_prevalence_by_phylum.png)
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

text: Across 27,690 GTDB species, 21.9% carry phaC and 21.7% have a complete PHB pathway; eggNOG annotations identified 118,513 PHB-related gene clusters across 19,496 species.
quote: Across 27,690 GTDB species, **21.9% carry phaC** (PHA synthase, the committed step for PHB biosynthesis) and **21.7% have a complete PHB pathway** (phaC + phaA/phaB). The near-identical prevalence of phaC-only and complete-pathway species indicates that virtually all phaC-carrying species also possess the upstream biosynthetic enzymes. A total of 118,513 PHB-related gene clusters were identified across 19,496 species using eggNOG annotations.
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

text: phaC is identified as PHA synthase, the committed step for PHB biosynthesis; its presence is used as a PHB pathway marker.
quote: Across 27,690 GTDB species, **21.9% carry phaC** (PHA synthase, the committed step for PHB biosynthesis) and **21.7% have a complete PHB pathway** (phaC + phaA/phaB). The near-identical prevalence of phaC-only and complete-pathway species indicates that virtually all phaC-carrying species also possess the upstream biosynthetic enzymes. A total of 118,513 PHB-related gene clusters were identified across 19,496 species using eggNOG annotations.
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

- **Pseudomonadota** dominates with 60.9% prevalence (4,544/7,456 species)
- **Myxococcota**: 52.9% (83/157)
- **Halobacteriota**: 34.4% (89/259)
- **Thermoproteota**: 27.9% (65/233)
- **Desulfobacterota**: 21.9% (70/319)

heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

text: No PHB was reported for Campylobacterota (0/271), Gemmatimonadota (0/102), Nanoarchaeota (0/135), or Marinisomatota (0/90); Patescibacteria was near zero at 0.4% (4/981).
quote: Several major phyla are entirely devoid of PHB: Campylobacterota (0/271), Gemmatimonadota (0/102), Nanoarchaeota (0/135), and Marinisomatota (0/90). Patescibacteria is near-zero at 0.4% (4/981), consistent with its reduced genome sizes and limited metabolic capacity.

text: Among orders with >20 species, 23 exceed 50% phaC prevalence, led by Azospirillales and Rhodospirillales (both 100%), Caulobacterales (99.3%), and Sphingomonadales (95.9%); 117 orders fall below 10%.
quote: At order level, 23 orders with >20 species exceed 50% phaC prevalence, led by Azospirillales and Rhodospirillales (both 100%), Caulobacterales (99.3%), and Sphingomonadales (95.9%). Conversely, 117 orders fall below 10%.
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

text: Figure phb_pathway_completeness.png summarizes 21.7% complete, 0.2% synthase-only, 46.5% precursors-only, 2.0% accessory-only, and 29.6% absent pathways.
quote: ![PHB pathway completeness across all 27K species, showing 21.7% complete, 0.2% synthase-only, 46.5% precursors-only, 2.0% accessory-only, and 29.6% absent](figures/phb_pathway_completeness.png)
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

text: The 46.5% precursors-only category is not PHB-specific because phaA (K00626) and phaB (K00023) are pleiotropic; phaR (K18080) was absent from eggNOG annotations for all 27K species, possibly owing to annotation coverage or misassignment.
quote: The large "precursors-only" category (46.5%) reflects the pleiotropic nature of phaA (beta-ketothiolase, K00626) and phaB (acetoacetyl-CoA reductase, K00023), which participate in general fatty acid and thiolase metabolism beyond PHB synthesis. Notably, phaR (K18080) was absent from all 27K species in the eggNOG annotations, suggesting either poor annotation coverage or misassignment of this regulatory gene.
heading: Finding 1: PHB pathways are widespread but phylogenetically concentrated

PHB prevalence varies dramatically by environment type across 27,690 species with classified primary environments:

| Environment | n species | % phaC | Expected variability |
|-------------|-----------|--------|---------------------|
| Plant-associated | 625 | 44.0% | High |
| Soil | 1,484 | 43.6% | High |
| Wastewater/engineered | 1,124 | 34.5% | High |
| Freshwater | 3,263 | 25.5% | Moderate |
| Sediment | 1,020 | 20.1% | Moderate |
| Marine | 3,010 | 18.7% | Low |
| Human associated | 1,237 | 11.1% | Low |
| Human clinical | 2,472 | 7.4% | Low |
| Animal associated | 3,711 | 3.3% | Low |
heading: Finding 2: PHB is enriched in environmentally variable habitats (H1a supported)

text: PHB presence was associated with the report's environmental-variability categories (chi2 = 1,656.36, p ~ 0, dof = 2), interpreted as enrichment in variable feast/famine habitats and depletion in stable or host-associated habitats.
quote: Chi-squared test for PHB presence x environmental variability category: **chi2 = 1,656.36, p ~ 0, dof = 2**. This strongly supports H1a: PHB pathway genes are enriched in bacterial clades from temporally variable "feast/famine" environments and depleted in stable or host-associated environments.
heading: Finding 2: PHB is enriched in environmentally variable habitats (H1a supported)

quote: ![Box plots showing AlphaEarth embedding variance for phaC+ vs phaC- species, with phaC+ species showing significantly higher environmental breadth (p=1.88e-06)](figures/embedding_variance_phb.png)
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: AlphaEarth provides 64-dimensional environmental embeddings for the niche-breadth proxy analysis.
quote: Using AlphaEarth environmental embeddings (64-dimensional vectors capturing environmental context) for 2,008 species with sufficient genome representation:
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: For 2,008 species with AlphaEarth embeddings, PHB+ species had median embedding variance 0.3295 (n = 531) versus 0.2472 for PHB− species (n = 1,477); Mann-Whitney U = 446,546, p = 1.88 x 10^-6.
quote:
Using AlphaEarth environmental embeddings (64-dimensional vectors capturing environmental context) for 2,008 species with sufficient genome representation:

- **PHB+ species** (phaC present): median embedding variance = **0.3295** (n = 531)
- **PHB- species** (phaC absent): median embedding variance = **0.2472** (n = 1,477)
- Mann-Whitney U = 446,546, **p = 1.88 x 10^-6**
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: PHB+ genomes were larger (median 4.34 Mbp vs 2.44 Mbp; rank-biserial r = -0.592, p ~ 0), genome size correlated with niche breadth (rho = 0.302, p = 1.5e-43), and adjustment changed the PHB–breadth correlation from rho = 0.106 (p = 1.77e-06) to partial rho = -0.047 (p = 0.037), reported as a 56.3% effect-size reduction with sign reversal.
quote: However, PHB+ species also have substantially larger genomes (median 4.34 Mbp vs 2.44 Mbp for PHB-, rank-biserial r = -0.592, p ~ 0), and genome size itself correlates with niche breadth (rho = 0.302, p = 1.5e-43). After controlling for genome size via partial Spearman correlation, **the PHB-niche breadth association largely disappears**: partial rho = **-0.047** (p = 0.037), a **56.3% reduction** in effect size with a sign reversal compared to the raw correlation (rho = 0.106, p = 1.77e-06).
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: Figure genome_size_confound.png shows genome-size distributions, size versus niche breadth, and environmental enrichment within genome-size quartiles.
quote: ![Genome size confound analysis: size distributions (left), size vs niche breadth colored by PHB status (center), and PHB enrichment by environment within genome size quartiles (right)](figures/genome_size_confound.png)
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: The report concludes that the apparent PHB–niche-breadth association is substantially confounded by genome size and cannot independently support the feast/famine hypothesis.
quote: This means H1b (niche breadth) is substantially confounded by genome size and cannot be interpreted as independent evidence for the feast/famine hypothesis. Larger genomes encode more metabolic pathways generally, and PHB is one of many pathways enriched in larger-genome species.
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: Within genome-size quartiles, high- versus low-variability phaC prevalence remained enriched: Q1 0.4–1.8 Mbp, 10.7% vs 2.5%, 4.4x, p = 1.18 x 10^-11; Q2 1.8–2.5 Mbp, 18.5% vs 4.0%, 4.6x, p = 3.25 x 10^-47; Q3 2.5–3.7 Mbp, 34.3% vs 10.9%, 3.1x, p = 4.17 x 10^-70; Q4 3.7–14.0 Mbp, 50.9% vs 37.4%, 1.4x, p = 3.21 x 10^-14.
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: In the smallest genome quartile (0.4–1.8 Mbp), species from high-variability environments were 4.4x more likely to carry phaC than those from low-variability environments; the report interprets this as genome-size-independent environmental enrichment.
quote: Even among the smallest genomes (Q1, 0.4–1.8 Mbp), species from high-variability environments are 4.4x more likely to carry phaC than those from low-variability environments. This demonstrates that the environmental enrichment signal is independent of genome size.
heading: Finding 3: PHB-niche breadth association is largely explained by genome size (H1b qualified)

text: Named PHB-enriched families include Burkholderiaceae, Burkholderiaceae_B, Rhodocyclaceae, Caulobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae, Xanthobacteraceae, Rhodanobacteraceae, Legionellaceae, Mycobacteriaceae, Nocardioidaceae, Haloarculaceae, Natrialbaceae, Nitrosopumilaceae, Microcystaceae, and Bacillaceae_G.
quote: Enriched families are concentrated in Pseudomonadota (Burkholderiaceae, Burkholderiaceae_B, Rhodocyclaceae, Caulobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae, Xanthobacteraceae, Rhodanobacteraceae, Legionellaceae) but also appear in Actinomycetota (Mycobacteriaceae, Nocardioidaceae), Halobacteriota (Haloarculaceae, Natrialbaceae), Thermoproteota (Nitrosopumilaceae), Cyanobacteriota (Microcystaceae), and Bacillota (Bacillaceae_G).

text: Enriched families skewed toward freshwater (5/41) and wastewater (3/41); depleted families skewed toward marine (18/62) and host-associated (12/62).
quote:
Environment distribution of enriched vs depleted families shows a clear pattern:
- **Enriched families** skew toward freshwater (5/41) and wastewater (3/41)
- **Depleted families** skew toward marine (18/62) and host-associated (12/62)
heading: Finding 4: Subclade enrichment reveals heterogeneous selection within phyla (H1d partially supported)

text: Family-level environmental interpretation is limited by sparse metadata: the other_unknown category covers 30/41 enriched and 26/62 depleted families.
quote: However, interpretation is limited by the dominance of the "other_unknown" category (30/41 enriched, 26/62 depleted), reflecting sparse environmental metadata for many species.
heading: Finding 4: Subclade enrichment reveals heterogeneous selection within phyla (H1d partially supported)

text: Phylogenetically discordant phaC presence yielded 311 potential horizontal gene transfer acquisition events in families with <20% phaC prevalence and 278 potential losses in families with >80% prevalence; these are potential, not confirmed, events.
quote:
Analysis of phylogenetically discordant phaC presence identified:

- **311 potential HGT acquisition events**: species carrying phaC despite being in families with <20% phaC prevalence
- **278 potential HGT loss events**: species lacking phaC in families with >80% prevalence
heading: Finding 5: Strong signal of horizontal gene transfer in phaC distribution

text: Among 311 discordant phaC-positive species, 60.1% carried phaC as accessory genome, versus 32.3% among all phaC-carrying species, supporting but not directly proving horizontal acquisition.
quote: Among the 311 discordant phaC-positive species, **60.1% carry phaC as accessory genome** (not present in all strains), compared to 32.3% accessory rate across all phaC-carrying species — nearly double. This strongly supports horizontal acquisition: recently transferred genes have not yet been fixed in the core genome.
heading: Finding 5: Strong signal of horizontal gene transfer in phaC distribution

text: Top families for putative phaC acquisition were Lachnospiraceae (38; family phaC 3.1%), Chitinophagaceae (22; 12.4%), Pelagibacteraceae (13; 5.3%), Enterobacteriaceae (11; 2.3%), and Planococcaceae (10; 12.8%).
quote:
Top recipient families for putative HGT-acquired phaC:
| Family | n acquisitions | Family phaC % |
|--------|---------------|---------------|
| Lachnospiraceae | 38 | 3.1% |
| Chitinophagaceae | 22 | 12.4% |
| Pelagibacteraceae | 13 | 5.3% |
| Enterobacteriaceae | 11 | 2.3% |
| Planococcaceae | 10 | 12.8% |
heading: Finding 5: Strong signal of horizontal gene transfer in phaC distribution

quote: ![phaC core vs accessory status by phylum, showing most phyla have predominantly core phaC, but some (SAR324, Bacillota_A, Eremiobacterota, Desulfobacterota) have high accessory fractions](figures/phb_core_vs_accessory.png)

text: The report highlights SAR324, Bacillota_A, and Eremiobacterota as high-accessory phaC lineages; overall 5,371 species carry core phaC and 1,959 accessory phaC, with some species carrying both.
quote: The high accessory fraction in SAR324, Bacillota_A, and Eremiobacterota suggests these lineages are active recipients of phaC via HGT. Overall, 5,371 species carry phaC as core and 1,959 as accessory (some species have both core and accessory copies).

text: Figure nmdc_phb_by_environment.png shows PHB inference-score distribution across 6,365 NMDC samples and pangenome matching coverage.
quote: ![Distribution of PHB inference scores across 6,365 NMDC samples (left) and pangenome matching coverage (right)](figures/nmdc_phb_by_environment.png)
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: Two-tier taxonomy matching mapped 3,014/3,492 (86.3%) NMDC taxon columns to GTDB genera of known PHB status; inference scores were abundance-weighted genus-level phaC prevalence over 6,365 NMDC metagenomic samples, with median 87.2% of taxonomic abundance matched.
quote: Using a two-tier taxonomy mapping (Tier 1: `gtdb_metadata` NCBI taxid → GTDB genus bridge, 2,336 taxon columns; Tier 2: direct genus name matching via `taxonomy_dim`, 678 additional columns), we successfully mapped **3,014/3,492 (86.3%) NMDC taxon columns** to GTDB genera with known PHB status. Per-sample PHB inference scores were computed as the abundance-weighted sum of genus-level phaC prevalence across 6,365 NMDC metagenomic samples, with a median 87.2% of taxonomic abundance matched to pangenome genera.
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: NMDC metagenomic samples and GTDB genus assignments were used for abundance-weighted inference of PHB capacity, not direct PHB measurement.
quote: Using a two-tier taxonomy mapping (Tier 1: `gtdb_metadata` NCBI taxid → GTDB genus bridge, 2,336 taxon columns; Tier 2: direct genus name matching via `taxonomy_dim`, 678 additional columns), we successfully mapped **3,014/3,492 (86.3%) NMDC taxon columns** to GTDB genera with known PHB status. Per-sample PHB inference scores were computed as the abundance-weighted sum of genus-level phaC prevalence across 6,365 NMDC metagenomic samples, with a median 87.2% of taxonomic abundance matched to pangenome genera.
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: Figure nmdc_phb_vs_abiotic.png displays inferred PHB scores against depth, temperature, maximum depth, and minimum depth.
quote: ![PHB inference score vs top abiotic correlates: depth, temperature, maximum depth, and minimum depth](figures/nmdc_phb_vs_abiotic.png)
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: PHB inference scores correlated with depth (rho -0.119, p 1.14 x 10^-21), temperature (+0.088, 1.86 x 10^-12), maximum depth (+0.076, 1.15 x 10^-9), minimum depth (-0.055, 1.05 x 10^-5), pH (+0.049, 7.95 x 10^-5), and ammonium nitrogen (+0.044, 4.49 x 10^-4).
quote:
PHB inference scores showed significant Spearman correlations with several abiotic variables:

| Abiotic variable | rho | p-value |
|-----------------|-----|---------|
| Depth | -0.119 | 1.14 x 10^-21 |
| Temperature | +0.088 | 1.86 x 10^-12 |
| Maximum depth | +0.076 | 1.15 x 10^-9 |
| Minimum depth | -0.055 | 1.05 x 10^-5 |
| pH | +0.049 | 7.95 x 10^-5 |
| Ammonium nitrogen | +0.044 | 4.49 x 10^-4 |
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: Abiotic correlation effect sizes were modest (|rho| < 0.12), and the report notes that NMDC point-in-time abiotic measurements are not direct measurements of temporal variability; depth and temperature interpretations are inferential.
quote: The negative correlation with depth is consistent with the feast/famine hypothesis: surface environments experience greater temporal variability in carbon inputs than deep subsurface, and communities in shallower samples carry higher inferred PHB capacity. The positive correlation with temperature aligns with expectations — warmer environments tend to have higher metabolic turnover and more dynamic carbon cycling. However, effect sizes are modest (|rho| < 0.12), likely reflecting that NMDC abiotic measurements are point-in-time snapshots rather than measures of temporal variability.
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: Across 693 genera matched between pangenome and NMDC metagenomes, PHB-high genera (>=50% phaC prevalence) had higher NMDC abundance than PHB-low genera (Mann-Whitney p = 8.41 x 10^-22); named high-abundance PHB-high genera were Mycobacterium, Pseudomonas, Cupriavidus, Burkholderia, and Methylobacterium.
quote: A genus-level cross-validation in NB05 provided stronger support: 693 genera were matched between the pangenome and NMDC metagenomes, and PHB-high genera (>=50% phaC prevalence) had significantly higher abundance in NMDC samples than PHB-low genera (**Mann-Whitney p = 8.41 x 10^-22**). Top PHB-high genera by NMDC abundance include *Mycobacterium*, *Pseudomonas*, *Cupriavidus*, *Burkholderia*, and *Methylobacterium* — all well-characterized PHB producers.
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: Figure pangenome_vs_metagenome.png compares pangenome PHB prevalence with NMDC metagenomic abundance and PHB-high versus PHB-low genus abundance.
quote: ![Pangenome PHB prevalence vs NMDC metagenomic abundance (left) and abundance comparison of PHB-high vs PHB-low genera (right)](figures/pangenome_vs_metagenome.png)
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: PHA synthase class analysis failed to resolve classes: all 11,792 phaC clusters were classified as other_pfam because the eggNOG PFAMs column used domain names (Abhydrolase_1, PhaC_N) rather than expected Pfam accession IDs (PF00561, PF07167).
quote: The PHA synthase class analysis classified all 11,792 phaC clusters as "other_pfam" because the eggNOG PFAMs column uses domain names (Abhydrolase_1, PhaC_N) rather than Pfam accession IDs (PF00561, PF07167) that the classification code expected. This remains a limitation.
heading: Finding 6: NMDC metagenomic cross-validation supports pangenome PHB patterns (H1c supported)

text: PHB-related gene and KEGG KO identities with cluster/species counts: phaA K00626 86,318/17,969; phaC K03821 11,792/6,067; phaB K00023 9,617/6,977; phaP K14205 6,130/4,571; phaZ K05973 4,656/3,151; phaR K18080 0/0.
quote:
| phaA | K00626 | 86,318 | 17,969 | Beta-ketothiolase (pleiotropic) |
| phaC | K03821 | 11,792 | 6,067 | PHA synthase (committed step) |
| phaB | K00023 | 9,617 | 6,977 | Acetoacetyl-CoA reductase (pleiotropic) |
| phaP | K14205 | 6,130 | 4,571 | Phasin (granule protein) |
| phaZ | K05973 | 4,656 | 3,151 | PHB depolymerase |
| phaR | K18080 | 0 | 0 | Transcriptional regulator |
heading: PHB Gene Discovery (NB01)

text: Pathway categories were complete (6,005 species), synthase-only (62), precursors-only (12,869), accessory-only (555), and absent (8,199); phaR was undetected and the report flags potential eggNOG underrepresentation.
quote: Species were classified by pathway completeness: complete (phaC + phaA/phaB, 6,005 species), synthase-only (phaC without precursor enzymes, 62), precursors-only (phaA/phaB without phaC, 12,869), accessory-only (phaP/phaZ/phaR without synthase, 555), and absent (8,199). The 5/6 detection rate for PHB KOs (phaR absent) suggests K18080 may be underrepresented in eggNOG annotations.
heading: PHB Gene Discovery (NB01)

text: The 6,067 phaC-carrying species span 95 of 142 GTDB phyla, and Pseudomonadota accounts for 74.9% (4,544/6,067). The report states that five named phyla account for 85.5% of carriers and 30.4% of species diversity, but its phylum counts above sum to 4,851/6,067 carriers, which does not equal 85.5%; this internal numerical contradiction remains unresolved.
quote: The 6,067 phaC-carrying species span 95 of 142 GTDB phyla but are concentrated in a few lineages. Pseudomonadota alone accounts for 74.9% of all phaC-carrying species (4,544/6,067), driven by high prevalence across Alpha- and Gammaproteobacteria orders. The five most PHB-enriched phyla (Pseudomonadota, Myxococcota, Halobacteriota, Thermoproteota, Desulfobacterota) together account for 85.5% of phaC+ species despite comprising only 30.4% of total species diversity.
heading: Phylogenetic Distribution (NB02)

text: Environment metadata covered 293,050 genomes spanning all 27,690 species; environment classes were harmonized from NCBI isolation_source, env_broad_scale, env_local_scale, and host fields into 11 categories.
quote: Environment metadata was available for 293,050 genomes spanning all 27,690 species. Environment classifications were harmonized from NCBI isolation_source, env_broad_scale, env_local_scale, and host fields into 11 categories. The gradient from high-variability environments (plant 44%, soil 43.6%) to low-variability environments (clinical 7.4%, animal 3.3%) represents a >10-fold difference in PHB prevalence, with a highly significant chi-squared association (chi2 = 1,656.36, p ~ 0).
heading: Environmental Correlation (NB03)

text: AlphaEarth embedding variance was a proxy for environmental breadth, based on 2,008 species with a minimum of 5 genomes per species with embeddings; the initial PHB+/PHB− difference persisted when restricted to phyla containing both groups.
quote: AlphaEarth embeddings provided an independent measure of environmental breadth for 2,008 species with sufficient genome coverage (minimum 5 genomes per species with embeddings). The embedding variance captures within-species variation in environmental context, serving as a proxy for niche breadth. The significant difference between PHB+ and PHB- species (Mann-Whitney p = 1.88e-06) held even after restricting to phyla with both PHB+ and PHB- representatives.
heading: Environmental Correlation (NB03)

text: The family-level analysis required >=10 species per family; among 248 eligible families, 41 were enriched and 62 depleted after Bonferroni correction.
quote: The family-level Fisher's exact tests (248 families with >=10 species) identified substantial heterogeneity: 41 enriched and 62 depleted families after Bonferroni correction.
heading: Subclade Enrichment and HGT (NB05)

text: Pangenome core/accessory status was defined by >90% genome prevalence within a species for core gene clusters and otherwise accessory; elevated accessory phaC in discordant species is indirect pangenome-scale evidence for horizontal transfer.
quote: The HGT analysis leveraged core/accessory classification from the pangenome: a gene cluster present in >90% of genomes within a species is "core," otherwise "accessory." The significantly elevated accessory rate in phylogenetically discordant species (60.1% vs 32.3%) provides pangenome-scale evidence for ongoing horizontal transfer of phaC, consistent with earlier single-species case studies (Kalia et al. 2007; Catone et al. 2014).
heading: Subclade Enrichment and HGT (NB05)

text: A gene cluster is classified as core if present in >90% of genomes within a species; otherwise it is accessory.
quote: a gene cluster present in >90% of genomes within a species is "core," otherwise "accessory."
heading: Subclade Enrichment and HGT (NB05)

text: The 60.1% accessory rate in phylogenetically discordant species, versus 32.3% overall, is indirect evidence of phaC horizontal transfer.
quote: The significantly elevated accessory rate in phylogenetically discordant species (60.1% vs 32.3%) provides pangenome-scale evidence for ongoing horizontal transfer of phaC
heading: Subclade Enrichment and HGT (NB05)

text: The feast/famine hypothesis predicts a PHB advantage under temporal carbon fluctuation.
quote: The classical feast/famine hypothesis (Dawes & Senior 1973) proposes that PHB is most advantageous under temporal carbon fluctuation.
heading: The Feast/Famine Hypothesis at Pangenome Scale

text: The report frames its 27,690-species survey as a pan-bacterial genomic test of the feast/famine hypothesis.
quote: Our data provide the first pan-bacterial genomic test of this hypothesis across 27,690 species and strongly support it:
heading: The Feast/Famine Hypothesis at Pangenome Scale
